idiom_name: JPA/Hibernate persistence context on the JVM (dirty checking + flush)
implementation_notes: On the JVM Kotlin uses the same unit of work as Java: an EntityManager's persistence context tracks managed entities, dirty checking finds modifications, and the state is synchronised on flush or at transaction commit, with Spring's @Transactional or JTA defining the boundary - Kotlin code reads the same and gains nothing by wrapping it. JetBrains' Exposed deliberately stops at the boundary: transaction { } runs the block on one connection, commits on normal completion and rolls back on exception, nested blocks share the parent unless useNestedTransactions is enabled, and savepoints are reachable through the connection property - but DSL and DAO writes execute immediately, so there is no identity map and no deferred flush. Use Exposed's transaction block for a statement-oriented service, JPA for a tracked object graph.
pitfalls: An EntityManager must not be shared across coroutines running on different threads; keep the persistence context inside one thread or use a coroutine-aware transaction manager.
Exposed's transaction { } blocks are synchronous on the calling thread - use suspendTransaction from exposed-r2dbc in coroutine-based services.
Exposed nested transaction blocks share the parent by default (useNestedTransactions = false), so an inner rollback discards the outer work too.
Lazy JPA associations touched outside the persistence context throw, and the classic fix (open session in view) keeps a context and connection open for the whole request.

variants.name: Exposed transaction { } with immediate DSL/DAO writes
variants.implementation_notes: Exposed wraps a block in a database transaction: commit on normal exit, rollback on exception, savepoints via connection.setSavepoint, and optional retries through maxAttempts - but every DSL or DAO statement is executed when it is called, so the unit of work is the block plus whatever change tracking you add. Prefer it for services that are statement-oriented and already use Exposed; add an explicit change set if you need ordered, deferred writes.
pitfalls: Entities stick to the transaction that loaded them, so cross-database references and entities used outside their transaction throw.
A rollback inside a nested block rolls back the parent as well unless useNestedTransactions is enabled, which is easy to misread as savepoint semantics.
